projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Szakacs was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history interview of John Szakacs. Mr. Szakacs served in the U.S. Navy and his highest rank was Radarman 3rd class. John served in the Pacific theater. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made in Mr. Szakacs home in North Royalton, Ohio, on April 8, 2003. John was 76 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: 1941? I was living in the small town in the southern part of Ohio, which is Warren, Ohio. And that's -- that's where I -- I was born in Leechburg, Pennsylvania, but we moved to Warren when I was about 7, and I finished school in Warren, and I was drafted into the service while I was residing in Warren.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But see you would -- you are -- you're having a birthday tomorrow --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- right?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Happy birthday in advance. You'll be 77 tomorrow?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see, so 19 --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: I was 18.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You -- but you were 15 when the Japanese attacked Pear Harbor, correct?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Approximately, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Still in school?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yes, mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of that day, of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, not really. Just like most people, I guess, but I was a kid, so it wasn't that important. I do remember, though right after the Sullivan brothers were lost in the Navy I went to enlist in the Navy. That was before I graduated from high school, and they turned me down. They told me to go back to school. And he says, "Don't worry," he says, "wait till you're drafted." I said, "But I want to get in the Navy," and he says, "Don't worry. You'll have a choice." So as it turned out, I did. I waited till I was 18, and I was drafted right afterwards, and I was -- my birthday was in April, well, of course, and I was -- and then I was sworn in on June the 10th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, before you were drafted, when you were still in high school, did you do anything for the war effort? Do you remember getting involved in anything like scrap drives or anything like that in high school?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: I did work part-time at the Lordstown Ordnance Depot, and we were receiving and loading material for the war -- for the army that was shipped overseas, all kind of equipment and so forth. And I worked there for, oh, until just about what -- almost until I went in the service, but that was -- that was about the extent of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you know, do you remember rationing being much of a problem?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, it wasn't a problem, but I remember the rationing, all the cards for gasoline and for the various food items, but being a young fellow like I was, you know, you didn't -- you was more interested in -- in having a good time --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. So you were draft -- you went into the service in June of '44, correct?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: June 10th I was -- went in -- sworn in. I was sworn in in Cleveland here, Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Tell me what --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: And I went in -- and I went into -- went -- went to the Great Lakes Naval Training Station. Believe it or not I had all of five weeks training. Five weeks. That's all we had at that time. You know, in -- the Army, you know, usually has a year's training. I had five -- five weeks training. I got my ten-day leave to come home. After my ten days was up I jumped on a train, went to California, ended up in -- in Oakland, and then Oakland is where I picked up the aircraft carrier USS Philippines, and I was a passenger with 600 other guys, and we headed overseas. And we went directly -- went directly across the Pacific. We never -- we thought we'd stop at Pearl Harbor. We never did. We went right on through to New Guinea, and it was -- it was called Hollandia Bay. It was shortly after the Americans secured the island that we arrived there. And there again I was assigned to a -- a bunk on the island, because my ship wasn't there yet. So we had to wait about two weeks before the ship -- our ship came in. So we were on K -- different -- KP duties and different things while we were waiting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that pretty tough, when you were -- went into the Navy and were thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, not really. I don't know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not much of an adjustment?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Not for me, it wasn't, no. I know -- I know at boot camp I know you heard -- you heard stories about a lot of guys -- young fellas in there crying at night, you know, because they missed their home and that, but I don't know, for some reason it didn't bother me. {Laughing}. It was -- I -- it started off as a great adventure, you know. Well, like most young fellas, you didn't worry about going in and being shot at or anything like that, so it was -- it was exciting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual happen during your five weeks of training?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No. Nothing -- nothing -- Everything was real fast, you know. One -- one or two days you went and learned how to tie knots, a couple days you went to learn the silhouettes of Japanese planes and ships, and then a couple days you went -- one day I think we had -- or two days swimming, they taught you how to swim and how to float and how to make a -- a floating gear in case you were overboard with your -- with your jeans. I don't know if you knew how they did that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, how did they do that?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, you -- if you didn't have a -- a life jacket, you took your jeans off in the water and you tied a knot in each leg and then held it open on top and then you brought it up over your head and brought it down this way, and it filled up with air, the two legs, and then you wrapped it around your stomach here, and it -- and then you were able to float. It held your weight. And eventually the air would leak out, but then you'd do it again and you continue doing that until hopefully somebody picked you up. But it saved a lot of guys' lives, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was like a homemade Made West -- Mae West?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, it was a life preserver, so to speak yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So -- And that was -- well, then we went to the dentist. We had to get our teeth checked. I had to have a tooth pulled. And of course, there was a lot of drill, a lot of calisthenics and running, and I think we spent one day on the rifle range. That was it. Of course, we -- the Navy, you don't have to learn -- you don't have to be a marksman, you know. That was the only time I ever fired a rifle. So actually it went real -- real quick, five weeks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What job were you trained for?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Nothing at -- at --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That point?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, they didn't train you for anything except they were just anxious to get you through basic training, I guess, whatever it was, but no -- no specific training. Most of us people were -- some people were, I guess, assigned to training schools, but I wasn't. And the odd -- another odd story I have here is from Warren, Ohio. There was only about 30,000 people in the -- in the small town. I don't know if you're familiar with Warren?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: There were five of us from Warren that were taken into the service at the same time. And we went through boot camp together, all five of us, and all five of us were assigned to the USS WARD. We went overseas together. And this was very unusual, especially after the Sullivan brothers were killed, and here there was five of us from this small town all assigned to this tiny little ship. And I don't know if I'm jumping ahead of myself, but when I did pick up my ship in -- in New Guinea, we were -- we were all four assigned to the USS Ward DD139, and we sat there waiting for orders, and before the orders came in four of us were transferred to the USS Schley. One fellow stayed behind on the Ward.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't actually spend any time on the Ward, or --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, we were on the Ward.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- for a while. For how long were you on the Ward?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Maybe -- Oh, I don't know, it seems a very short time, because we never left -- we never went out to sea on the Ward, just sat there at the dock for a couple of weeks waiting for orders to come in from wherever they came from. So actually I -- before we went out I was transferred to the Schley, so just long enough on there to have the Ward on my records.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So it would have -- it would have been -- well, fortunately for me that we were transferred to the Schley, because we never received any -- any damages or any -- any losses, but our fella -- the other fella that stayed on the Ward from Warren, well, of course, he was -- his ship was sunk, you know, later on and he got to go home. But luckily there was no one killed that day -- on that day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you got over to New Guinea probably what, July or August of '44; would that be right?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No. Because we -- I crossed the equator --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- crossed --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me about the ceremony for crossing the equator.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, that's a long story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: You don't want to hear that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you can hit the highlights.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, let's see here. The 17th of September, 1944, I crossed -- crossed the equator.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So that didn't give me -- from the time I got in June 10th to September, and here I was already crossing the equator.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, that didn't give me -- didn't give us much time for anything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So anyhow, we didn't know it at the time, but now that I look back I realize that they were getting as many people as they could into the Navy in preparation for the big invasion of -- of Leyte, you know, the Philippines. So anyhow, that's -- What was your other question?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, well, I was going to ask for the highlights of the --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, the ceremony.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, it was -- it was -- it was interesting, but first, for about -- about a week before we crossed the equator, you know, they would -- the fellas that were already in -- had crossed before, they're called shell backs, and if you hadn't never crossed you were called a pollywog. So about a week before on the loudspeaker system they would -- they would -- someone -- someone would always come on there and make up stories of "Beware, pollywogs, the day is coming," you know, and all this kind of stuff. They would try to scare you. And there was 600 of us. You know, this included regular seamen and officers too that had never crossed. So the final day came, they -- they initiated the officers first, and that was -- that was horrible. Well, I don't know if you want to know all the details how they set you in the -- first of all they would -- we had a -- I remember going -- going through this tunnel. It was like a box or tunnel, and it was full of garbage and all kind of stuff. You had to crawl through it, and then you had to crawl over to the -- King Neptune. He was a -- he was a -- sitting on the throne, and he was a big guy like you, only he didn't -- all he had was shorts on, and you had to go up and kiss his stomach. And -- and then there the guy -- from there basically you went into a barber's chair. They had a barber's chair set up, and a guy would throw some stuff in your face and your hair and that and then -- then he would give you a push, and the chair would tip over and you'd fall. It was a carrier, so they had you on the edge of the deck -- flight deck, and you were on it -- the elevator -- on the edge of the elevator was down, and you fell down into this big tank of water, and there would be about three or four guys down in there that was shell backs, and they would grab you as you fell in and they'd dunk you. And then they -- as they brought you up then they'd holler "Shell back or pollywog?" And then if you didn't holler "Shell back" they'd dunk you again, and they held you down longer. So finally when you come up and hollered "Shell back," then they'd throw you out, and there's a big long line of -- of sailors, shell backs, along the deck, two row -- two rows of them, and you had to run down between them, and they had paddles. And then they would -- as you ran down they'd swipe at you, try to hit you, and you would try to get through there as fast as you could. And that was basically what it was. But the officers, they -- they were -- I was amazed that some of them were stubborn. I remember seeing one -- one officer, he wouldn't holler "Shell back," and I thought they were going to drown him. They must have dunked him about a half a dozen times, and each time they'd hold him down there longer. And then when he -- he finally came up and -- and running through that gauntlet, he didn't run. He crawled on his hands and knees just in spite, and they were whacking the heck out of him. And -- and all us guys were watching and says, "Man, if they do that to officers, they're gonna kill us." But, of course, they had to do it in one day and there was 600 of us, so they speeded up the process a little bit for us, fortunately, {laughing}. So anyway, that's how that happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And this all began basically the moment you crossed the equator?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right. That one day. It took -- you started in the morning and you finished up by evening.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So anyhow, it was quite interesting. And it -- so -- so from there it was -- we -- it was uneventful. We went -- we had drills on the way over the Pacific, you know, during the -- during the day at times, but nothing ever transpired. We -- we thought maybe the worst thing would happen would be a Japanese submarine, but we never did -- we made it to New Guinea. We disembarked and -- and were stationed on the island there for, I don't know, maybe it was a week before the Ward came in. And they posted us -- our names on the bulletin board. We had to check it every day and make sure your ship was come -- had come in and you reported. So -- But anyhow, from the time I left the Ward then and was assigned to the Schley APD 14, and then we sat there for maybe a week and our orders finally came in, and that's -- that's where this story begins, on our first operation, which was called Dinagat Operation. Now, this -- what it -- what it entailed -- basically, what it entailed was we loaded up with 150 Ranger -- Rangers and we went -- left Hollandia -- I don't know the exact date -- with four other APD's like ourselves.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell us again what APD -- I don't think we got that on tape. What -- what does that mean, APD?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: All purpose destroyer. We were -- it was -- and we were assigned -- it was -- it was an amphibious -- we were with the 7th Fleet Amphibious Corps.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many troops would you carry?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Between 150 and 200.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you had craft --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: They were landing -- Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had landing craft on the -- how many landing craft?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Four. Two on each side. When they reconverted it to a two stack they removed the -- the original torpedo tubes, and that's where the -- the landing craft were hung.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And all the APD's were former World War I destroyers --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- is that correct?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right. They were all former -- if you recall, our -- before we got into the war Roosevelt sent 50 of these over to England, and that's what it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah. To interrupt my story again, when I -- when I came home from the service my first job -- well, my first job was as a junior draftsman, and I went to work at -- UNKNOWN FEMALE: Bartlett & Snow? SZAKACS: -- Bartlett & Snow as a junior draftsman, and see this -- SWOPE: Mm-hmm. SZAKACS: -- USS Schley, well it was summertime and I was working there like this, and I was drawing, and the chief draftsman -- this was about -- about maybe a week -- chief draftsman George Johnson, he was about 45 years old or so, come walk -- come by and he sees my tattoo and he says, "USS Schley? You were on that?" And I says, "Yeah." He says, "What was that?" I says, "Well, it was an APD." He says, "You know what, I served on that in World War I."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}. Wow.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah. He asked me all about it. I said, "Yeah, it's still the same," you know, and he says, "Yeah, I was on that in World War I in the Mediterranean," and he says, "We were one of the fastest ships afloat." It was amazing, you know, that I would run into somebody like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So -- It was -- it was quite awesome there. It was interesting the -- the -- the destroyer was quite a -- quite a unique ship. It was -- You could see how small it is. I think it was only 305 feet long and about 35 feet across. That's all it was. And then you read -- Well, it only drew about seven feet of water, and you could see by these pictures where it's sitting in the water, it's very low in the water -- sitting in the water, and -- Oh, what was I going to say -- oh, it wasn't like a -- a normal -- what do I want to say -- a standard destroyer, one of these new fletchers that came out during the war. We had -- On the new type destroyers or any ship after that, particularly when you went to chow, you went down in the galley and then you stood in line and you took a tray and you went through and they threw food on your tray and you went -- went off and -- and sat down and ate it, where on this ship each compartment where we -- where we bunked, we'd have two bunks on each side, and in the center there was a long table in the compartment, and we would fold the bunks up, and there was lockers, and you sat on these lockers and you were sat then at a table just like here, and your food was brought down from the galley. The table was all set, and it was sat down, and the Chief Bosun Mate would be on the end. He would start. He'd take his first, and then they'd pass the food down, and then we'd go down and around, and when you got through eating you just left everything this way and you got up and left and a mess boy would come by and pick everything up and clean -- clean it up and set up for the next meal. So it was like being at home. It was unusual.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: If you were at the end of the table would you get shorted a little bit?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, just --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Everybody was fair --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, because they always brought down more food.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: That's one thing -- Most of the time we got pretty good food in the Navy, except when we were out -- out at sea for a long period of time and we'd start running low, and then we'd -- we'd have to look for a supply ship to take on more provisions. But yeah, I tell -- I tell this to other -- other guys that I meet in the Navy and they can't believe that we ate -- that that was how we lived, you know, that's neat. So that was only -- only to the World War I that they built them that way. I don't know if all the other ones -- but anyway, the fact that we were, you know, such a small ship, but it was very seaworthy. At one time we rode out a typhoon in the Pacific. I don't know if they -- I don't know what the dates were. We were -- we were -- if we were going to Okinawa or where it was, but we rode -- we hit this severe Typhoon, and the ship was rolling and pitching. Alongside of us in a distance there was some new destroyers, the fletch -- they called the fletcher type destroyers, and they were -- you could see them -- when they went up like this you could see the radar dome underneath -- underneath. It'd come down, and -- and -- and when we were rolling over we could take -- I don't know how -- how much roll we could take, and then we'd go down into those swells. I don't know if you've ever been on a ship --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, not like that.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- but when you going down -- when you go down in one of these swells the water comes right up along the edge of the ship almost, and you look up -- you can look up about 30 or 40 feet and all you see is a solid wall of water, and then, of course, when you come out of this swell you come up, you ride the top of it, and then you look down -- down another 30, 40 feet. It was -- it was hair raising. But any way, we managed to ride through this -- through it. But later we heard that there was quite a few new fletcher type destroyers that were capsized. They were built too top heavy. We were built low, so we could take quite a bit of roll and not roll over. These guys were going -- they'd go over so far and they'd just topple over. A lot of guys were lost. The only thing we lost during that Typhoon was our anchor. The Captain thought he could -- we could ride the anchor, you know, they would drop the anchor and let it down to the bottom and then you'd just swing around the anchor, but what happened was the anchor went off dunked over the side, and it was like -- it was like a huge whale grabbed the anchor and took off with it, because it went straight out from the ship and it -- all of the chain came out of the -- out of the locker to the end, and it caught the end and it -- and it stopped -- well, it almost pulled the -- the mechanism out of the deck, but the chain was out horizontally in the water, you know, above the water, and it was straining and it was pulling us over, so one of the mechanics ran up forward with a blow torch and cut the chain, so we lost our anchor. So that -- that again -- that -- from then -- that was later on, though, this happened. We were -- I think we were on our way to Okinawa, so we couldn't -- we couldn't do certain -- we couldn't go into any harbors and -- and anchor anymore, you know what I mean, so most of the time, then, after that we were on picket duty, which would be just circling around outside perimeter of a -- of a -- of an area. So getting back -- getting back to this operation on Dinagat, we went -- there was five of us went on this operation, and we went -- actually we went there in October -- we left October 12th. We were task group 78.4, and they were -- I forget what group of Rangers we took along -- along with us. And our goal was to go there -- we went there -- we arrived at Dinagat, which was on the tip of Leyte Gulf, a little island. There were three little islands, and ours was Dinagat. We got -- we got to the island about -- it was actually A-3 days, so we were there three days before the main task force was coming in, and our job was to land the Rangers on the tip of the island, which had a radio and radar station. And they were supposed to go in and knock out the radio and radar so that the -- our main task force coming in the Leyte would not be detected. So we -- we landed the Rangers on the island and we were standing by, waiting for -- we were going to pick up casualties or anything that happened and taken them back -- back to Hollandia. And we waited there, oh, most of the morning, and nothing happened. And so we were waiting there, and all of a sudden we see a canoe coming out from the island, a dug-out canoe, with a couple of natives and what looked like to be a -- a Navy Lieutenant. And sure enough, that's what it was. He came over to us, and here it was a -- it was a Lieutenant -- actually, it was a Lieutenant -- Navy Lieutenant or Army Lieutenant -- I'm sorry -- because he was -- he was on the island when the Japanese invaded, and he managed to escape up into the mountains, and he joined up with the Philippine gorillas, and he lived there for -- well, for two years until we got back in there. And we was -- we offered to take him back with us -- take him with us, and he refused to go. He says no, he says, he's -- he met a Philippine girl while he was up in the mountains and he married her and he wanted to stay. So I said, "Well --" we said to him, "Well, is there anything you would like to have," you know, and he says all he wanted was an Army 45. I guess he lost his or whatever happened, but we got him a -- a 45 and some ammo. Turn the fan off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But he wanted to continue to fight with the gorillas and --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- didn't want to go back to the Army?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: I -- You know, that would be interesting to find out. I don't know if he eventually --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Or he just stayed there?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- he -- he eventually must have came back to the states with his -- with his wife --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- I imagine --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- you know, because the war was still -- he probably just wanted to finish out the war --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- up there in the mountains. So it was interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: But anyway, like I say, we were there three days before the main task force came in. We were practically sitting ducks there, because it was all occupied Japanese yet. The Japs had all their airfields there and their ship -- Japanese ships in the area, and so we were sweating it out for a couple -- we were there a couple of days, but on the last day we -- we decided they didn't need us there anymore, we turned -- turned and left, and that's when -- that's when we were going back and we seen this -- By the way, this story was in -- this story I had in -- was in the Plain Dealer --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- of that -- of that operation. It was uneventful as far as -- as far as the -- the operation went. The Rangers landed, and they found that the Jap -- the Philippine gorillas had already wiped out the radio and radar stations and killed all the Japs over there on that island -- on that particular part of the island that -- on the point there. So we just headed -- headed back to our original base then. That's when we -- the first day out we met coming in toward us -- that's when we seen the task force coming. It was something like 700 ships on the way there for the landing. That was quite a sight. Yeah --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the Rangers come back with you then?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No. No. They stayed on --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They stayed -- they stayed there --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- they stayed on the island, yeah, mm-hmm. No. We stood by in case -- in case they had a firefight, you know, if any of them were wounded, then we were going to put them on our landing craft and bring them back on board ship, because we had a -- we had a doctor on board, always carried a doctor, a -- a full doctor. Most -- a lot of ships didn't have doctors on them for some -- I don't know what reason we had one, but we had a doctor and a -- and a corpsman both. So -- so that was -- so then we just went back to -- to our base at -- at New Guinea and waited for further orders then. We got re-supplied and -- and waited. And so -- so actually our next -- our next operation, then, was -- was called Ormoc Raid. That was the southern part of Leyte, Ormoc Bay. I'm just trying to see here what we were -- This was -- I think -- I think this was -- this was when the -- yeah, this is -- this is the -- this is the day that -- the raid that the USS Ward was sunk, Ormoc. Actually we went up -- we went up there on -- it was December 7th, 1944, mm-hmm, and once again we landed -- this -- this time we landed the 1st Battalion Army's 305th Infantry troops destined for the first -- first wave. While up -- while up there at the -- After we disembarked our -- our troops they went on -- went on the shore and hit the beach, that's when we were attacked by the Japanese Air Force. Many Jap planes were coming in. They were all kamikazes, of course. Of course, we weren't alone on this operation. There were a lot of other ships -- a lot of LST's and other destroyers. There were two -- two of our ships were sunk. Let me see what the name of the -- the one -- the one L -- APD was the USS Mahan and the USS Ward both -- both were hit by -- by kamikaze. The Mahan sunk almost immediately and the Ward remained afloat, was burning. That's when the Captain from the O'Brien, new destroyer, was called in to sink her. We didn't -- because we had to leave and they didn't want to leave her behind, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did your ship have any close calls with kamikazes?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. We had many of them. This -- this day was -- was particularly heavy with the kamikazes, on the 7th. The Japs kept coming out all day long. Of course, we had good air coverage. We had -- Do you remember hearing about Major Bong?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Major --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Bong.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: You never heard of him? Oh, he was a famous --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I might have. I might have forgotten his name.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: He was -- he was a famous ace.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I might have heard of his exploits and forgot his name.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, he -- at this particular time he was on -- he had a P38 squadron under him. He was the leader --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- and they gave us protection most of the day. They were shooting the Jap planes as they tried to come down on the hit -- the ships, his fighters would dive in on them. And the -- on -- the one -- one occasion we -- we watched -- I think it was Major Bong who shot down two planes at one -- at -- at the same time. Not exactly the same time, but he dove down on two planes, got one, and as he pulled up he hit another one. So it -- it was actually fun watching these dogfights go on until you knew one of those plane -- one of those Jap -- Japanese kamikazes were heading for you. But they were -- some of them were shot down by artillery shells from the ships. Everybody was firing at them at one time. But they -- they were following us all day long. There was quite a few -- watched quite a few LST's and other APD's get hit. And we had a couple of close calls where -- whereby the kamikazes would miss us and hit in the water or hit something else alongside of us, another ship. One particular -- I was up on the flying bridge as -- as a spotter, and there's -- there was one kamikaze coming in dead on, dead -- heading -- heading right aimed for us, and there was a -- I think it was a Corsair that was on his tail, following him in, and we couldn't open fire because we were afraid of opening -- to hit -- hit our own plane, so we had to just sit there and wait. And he came in, the Corsair came in on his tail, and about 1,000 yards out he hit the -- the Jap plane, and the plane hit about -- only about, oh, maybe -- yeah, maybe about 1,000 -- not even 1,000 yards, hit the water in front of us, and, of course, as he was coming in I had these big binoculars, you know, I could see real good, and I swear I -- I -- I looked at that Jap, and I -- I -- that was real scary. I thought he was right on top of us. I had to take the glasses down to make sure he was still out there. But anyway, he crashed in the water, and as -- as he hit the water we went right over him. That's how close -- that was one of our closest encounters. So anyhow, we were happy when evening came then and the planes then didn't -- didn't go out at night, ours or -- or the Japanese. So anyway, from that -- the -- the mission, I guess, was -- as far as the Range -- the Army was concerned it was -- it was successful. They -- they reached their objectives there on the -- on the landing. Now , moving -- Oh, yeah, see, I have -- I have here that -- the totals here. We added up the six -- 62 Jap planes were shot down that day, ten by Naval fire and the others by Major Bong's P38 group and Corsairs. So that was -- that was that operation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you write these?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These are documents you got from elsewhere?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, these -- we were going -- we had -- we had a communication -- I think it was a communications officer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: That's why this is really good. They have all the details here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, so these are copies of things from the After Action Reports?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, he wrote these afterwards, when we got back to shore, where --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- where he would type these all up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So he had all the -- all the records of all these -- everything that happened, you know, the exact times and the -- and the exact vehicles that were there and the -- the planes and the other ships and the Rangers and the Army or whoever we had there. But so it was -- it's quite -- quite accurate. It was practically like belongs to the ship log.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was like they did those report after actions --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- too --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: These were -- My son typed these up for me from the originals. The originals that I had was on the -- it was like a tissue paper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I know. Yeah, I've got some of those documents.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Do you? Okay. They were getting pretty shabby.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very -- Exactly. Very fragile.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So I don't know how many years ago my youngest son typed them all over for me, so this is what -- these are the originals, I think -- no, this is a copy here. So they're quite accurate as far as -- as everything -- everything goes on, the outcome of everything. Of course, I mean, there -- there's -- I -- I don't -- I can't remember all the details, but he has them covered here pretty well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Once I went through and read it all. I'm just looking -- looking through and see if I missed anything important.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When your son typed these up he just typed them up word-for-word --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- he didn't change anything?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, no, huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you know when he did that, when he typed these up?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Approximately?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, I don't know how many years ago it's been. He has the originals yet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I just wondered, because I could send in copies of these to the Library of Congress. They ask roughly when these copies were made, and -- but if they're word-for-word from the original documents, I can send these in.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm. Yeah, these are -- these are word-for-word, mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Then I'll just --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So actually --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- I'll take a guess as to when they -- he -- he typed them up.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, it's been --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Four or five years ago, maybe? UNKNOWN FEMALE: About, I'd say -- SZAKACS: Yeah, he was already living over here on Bennet at the time -- UNKNOWN FEMALE: I'd say about five years. SWOPE: Five years ago? All right. SZAKACS: Mm-hmm. Something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. Yeah, as long as it's the original document retyped and it has the --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- fills in some of the information, so that's why --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Mm-hmm, yeah, it -- it goes into a lot of detail about the -- how they went into the -- other ships, what was very unique before they landed on the -- on shore, the Rangers or the Army, they had these small crafts that would cruise along -- along the shoreline, and they called them pulverizers, and they -- and they had bat -- big battery -- all they had was batteries of rocket launchers on each side, and they would just fire these all off, you know, big waves of those would just go out and hit the beach, and then they'd turn around and come back and empty the other side. You know, it was quite amazing to see, and you wonder how anything ever survived on shore, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How big were those?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: They were small ships --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Small --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- they were small ships, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- converted landing barges?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: They just had these racks of rocket launchers along the whole side -- on two sides. They just launched them all off. It'd only -- it'd only take a couple minutes and they'd be gone. So -- Anyway, I don't know if there's anything you want to ask -- ask me about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you can continue on. Now what -- what's the next operation?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was the second operation, right?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: A few days -- after a few days rest we made preparations to -- to go up into -- to -- not Opitz (ph) -- Mindoro. It's an island -- I don't know if there's -- I have a map here of it or not. I thought I did. It's the southern -- southern part of the Philippines. At this time we were under Admiral Struble, who was -- who was going to assemble the assault group. Our -- our land -- our landing group was spearheaded by four old APD's and four new APD's carrying in the first wave. The rest of the landing force were LCT's, LSM's and L -- LST's. Also the group contained some minesweeps. Group contained -- consisted of 22 destroyers and three light and one heavy cruiser. So -- I was trying to think -- remember now what the outstanding -- our --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was this operation?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: This was right after Ormoc.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Still in '44 or --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- was that in '45?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, no, no. Everything -- everything I'm telling you was still in '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Uh, this was probably -- I don't know if there's a -- this was December 7th --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- and this was just a few days later, so probably around maybe -- maybe a week later or a few days, about the 10th or so of December. I'm just trying to refresh my mind as to why -- what we were doing there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was your job spotter most of the time --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: My --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- during a battle --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: My battle station --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- that was your battle station?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- was up on a flying bridge, and I was in one of those swivel chairs with the binoculars, spotting -- mainly -- mainly it was planes as they were coming -- coming in. I'd designate where -- what are they were in, and I had a microphone, and the control officer was standing back there, and he would direct various guns to which planes to go for. But during -- during the working hours during the day I was in the radio shack, the radar -- radar -- radar and sonar -- I was a radar and sonar operator, so during the day that's my -- during the working hours that's what I did --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- operated the radar and the sonar, and then battle stations up on deck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Everybody had two duties.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Would they continue to operate radar and sonar when you were under attack or --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- or at that point you were fighting --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, no, not then --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- because when we're attacked everybody's -- everybody's up -- up above manning a gun or something or doing something, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there more than one radar sonar operator?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yes. Because we had -- we worked in shifts, you know, just like -- just like --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Sure.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- army.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So at least three, I guess?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah. Four.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Four?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Four -- no, four. We'd be on four hours --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Four hours?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- four hours on and -- and -- then we were off -- four and eight, four hours on, eight hours off. But this would be around the clock --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- so -- and then -- and then also part of my -- my duties were part of the time I'd be sitting up in the control center on -- on the ship and part of the time in the -- take over the wheel and -- on the helm and steer the ship. You know, all we had to do was look down and watch the -- watch the compass.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that like, to actually be steering the ship, even though you were --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, it was -- it was fun, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: It was -- oh, you've seen them, the big --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- the big wheel, you know. And we'd take turns. And the other -- when we weren't doing that we were -- there would be a little -- like a high chair inside there on the side, and you'd sit up there and wait our turn again. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- it was interesting. I forgot about that myself until just now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You forgot you steered the ship {laughing}?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah. And I -- Let's see here. What we -- anything important happen here -- I'm -- of course, we were -- on all these missions we were constantly under -- under other aircraft, you know, fire, attack from -- from the Japanese planes, no matter when we went out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any bodies on your ship?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No. Like I say, fortunately we never got hit by --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- by any Jap planes or -- or shells. We were at one time -- well, I don't want to jump ahead of myself here. There's a -- there's a lot -- there's a lot that's not in here. I was -- I'm trying to think of what the significance was of when we went to Mindoro -- END OF FILE SR0001001, BEGIN FILE SR0001002

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- other than just land -- land -- our troops were Company "B" of 503rd Paratroopers. They were grounded for the day and spent -- we were -- took them in as a amphibious landing --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- so actually -- actually all we were supposed to do going up there was taking these fellas in and hitting the beach. They were approximately 130 miles from Manila --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- when they went in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Manila was on Luzon, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Mm-hmm. We did -- really didn't encounter -- I -- as far as I could tell, we didn't encounter any -- anything too severe except, of course, we were always pestered by the Japanese fighter planes. So that's about all --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was all you can recall?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- that was all I could tell you about Mindoro, that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- we made the landing, and we were constantly under -- under attack by Japanese planes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: You know, once we land -- land our troops we wait and pick up the landing craft when they come back, and then we'd get out of the area as fast as we can.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: {Laughing}. So anyhow --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this next is, then, to Bataan?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah. Well, we -- yeah, we were -- we -- actually, we made the first landing back to Bataan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: We were the first group to land there. Let's see if -- if -- if they say the -- if I have a record here of who we took in. I don't know if they were Army Rangers -- no, it doesn't -- doesn't say -- my records don't -- don't say where it was, but I could -- there -- just all I -- we arrived -- after Mindoro we arrived at Subic Bay with our -- the other APD's, the Schley, the Kilty, the Crosby, the Manley, and the Talbot, and the operation took us under the guns of Corregidor for a landing at Mariveles Bay on the southern tip of Bataan. The -- the thing that I remember most -- most about this is that we were em -- disembarked our troops in the landing craft, and their staging area was -- I can't remember if it was on the left side of our ship. They would all come over from the other ship, all the landing craft, and they would circle around and circle until they all got together and then they would go in and hit the beach at the same time. Well, while they were gathering in this group one of the guns on Corregidor was still active, and it fired -- fired a shell at us. Actually -- well, either us or all the troops, but anyway, one of the -- he heard a shell coming in, and it hit in the midst of these landing crafts, and it -- I don't know if it destroyed or -- I can remember seeing it hit the water and damage some landing craft pretty bad. One of the -- one of the -- one of the Rangers were killed and there were several of them that were wounded. But anyway, the gun -- Are you familiar with the guns on Corregidor --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- on the -- up on the hillside?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: They were -- they were down in -- in -- in trenches in the -- buried in the ground. They'd come up on a track and they'd come up and fire a gun and the recoil would send them back down in, so you couldn't see where they came from. So they -- they -- we heard that one shell come in, and then another shell came in that landed on the -- on -- it landed on our port side in the water. It exploded and, of course, shrapnel came down, but that's all. Nobody got hurt from it. It just looked like -- it felt like a hailstorm, you know, coming down and tinkling all over the deck. Well, in the meantime one on this side and one on this side and we figured if they get another shell off they're going to have us zeroed in. And they did, they got another shell off, and it came and it landed a little closer but still on the port side, still in the water.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, that was all -- all -- all they had a chance for, because sitting out about ten miles out from -- from the rock there was a big cruiser, and all he did was sat there and looked through his binoculars and watched for these flashes, and then they would pinpoint after three -- three guns -- three times they had it pinpointed pretty well, because then these big ten inch guns on the cruiser opened up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: They must have went straight down that hole, because the gun never fired again at us. So that -- that was -- to me that was scary. All -- I would say on -- just about as frightening as a kamikaze coming in, you know, when you were sitting there waiting and you couldn't see where it come from, you just heard the shell coming in and then -- then watching it explode. So -- so, then, from -- after -- after -- after Bataan we had orders to go back into Subic Bay again -- this was -- and pick up some paratroopers. This was also -- this was, again, the 503rd --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- Paratroop Battalion jumped on Corregidor the day before, and what happened was they thought they were going to land -- land on that -- there was a -- I think there was a golf course or something up on top. They thought they were going to land on there. Well, what happened, they dropped all these paratroopers and the wind picked up, and all the -- most of them were blown over the side of the cliffs. So when we got -- got there it made -- the cliff was just covered with white parachutes. So -- but we had picked up additional paratroopers from Subic Bay and we were rushing them in and hit the beach, because they didn't want to take a chance on dropping any more. So we picked up about 150 para -- paratroopers and went up on -- over to the beach in the designated area and launched -- launched our boats and sent the -- sent some into the shoreline. There was a couple -- we didn't -- we didn't really -- we didn't receive any shell -- shells, but the -- the troops went in and they received quite a bit of fire from the Japs that were still there on the beach -- beach area, and we had a -- a destroyer come in close to the beach. I thought for sure he was going to ground it -- be grounded, he was -- came in so close. And he opened up on that beachhead where the Japs were pinned down and wiped them out. And -- and then our troops were able to continue on their operation. But -- so that was -- that was all -- that was -- that was all for -- for the Corregidor landing, actually, and the -- the only -- that's the only one I have documented, because then from -- from Corregidor we went back -- back to Leyte and re -- re -- we got outfitted again, and our new orders were then to leave Leyte, and by this time they had invaded Okinawa, so our next mission was to go up -- up there, and we were on escort duty and -- and then do some picket duty up there, circling around, because we didn't have -- we couldn't anchor up there. But anyway, we didn't carry any troops up there. On our way up there we did encounter a Japanese -- we thought -- well, I'm sure it was a Japanese submarine we picked up on sonar, and we -- we dropped a pattern of depth charges and -- but we didn't stick around to see if anything happened. We just continued on and got up to Okinawa. And we got up there at night, and -- we were on the outskirts of the bay or entrance to the bay there in Okinawa, and we know there was a lot of -- lot of ships that were hit, and particularly at night -- even at night the Japanese were coming in, the planes, because what they would do is they would come in right about -- right above the waterline in the dark, and you couldn't see them and they couldn't see you, but they didn't care. They just flew in above the water until they hit something. And they knew -- they knew when they hit they'd hit an American ship. And we also at the time knew there was -- there were some torpedo boats -- Japanese that were outfitted with torpedoes or -- or ammo in the front, and they would do the same thing. They would just cruise around in the bay area until they hit -- until they hit something. And, of course, the Jap -- some of the planes were -- came -- came in higher and we couldn't fire on them because we -- our -- our guns were -- were controlled by sight only, aimed by sight, where the new destroyers were -- had radar already controlled guns, so they could pick them up on radar and they could -- then the gun would automatically aim at the Japanese plane. So we were -- we were only there that -- that night for a short time. I don't -- I don't know why we went up there originally. Our duty was -- mainly was to escort some ships up there, but anyway, the other interesting thing that happened on our way back, we turned -- it was still night, it was pitch black out, and we were leaving the area, and maybe, oh, I don't know, maybe a couple of miles to our stern -- I don't know if you ever heard or recall the ship USS Comfort --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- that's the hospital ship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, she was -- we were the closest one to her, and she was all -- all lit up with lights all over her. It was at night, but she was all lit up, and any war ship in the area had to stay so many miles or yards away from the hospital ship or else -- that was -- I guess that was the law, the Geneva Conference, you know, war ships got to stay away. But anyway, she took a kamikaze that night, and we watched -- we watched -- we didn't hear -- see the plane, but we heard it and we heard the -- seen the explosion on the deck. And from what we understand, it had -- it hit right in the main operating room and killed a few doctors and nurses and some GI's that were in there. So that was the -- that was a terrible thing to witness, anyway. But I noticed the Comfort is still -- still in existence today. It's in -- in -- it's in the middle east now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: And, uh, from -- from there we went back to Leyte, and then from there we had orders -- orders to go back to the states for repairs, because we got -- had to get a new anchor, and I don't know what else we had to do, but on the way back we did stop at Pearl Harbor and unloaded -- unloaded all our ammo.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: And that's when I got -- went to shore and found a tailor shop and had all new clothes made, because I didn't have any clothes. All our GI issue I threw overboard. All we wore overseas was -- was dungarees, you know, most of them were cut-offs --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- because we were in the south Pacific, you know. One of the interesting things that I could -- that I could -- can recall, during -- during the lull in different operations, one -- one occasion we -- we stopped engines -- I don't know where it was, out in the middle of the Pacific someplace -- and we decided to have a beer -- beer party. So we lowered the landing crafts and -- because you couldn't drink beer onboard ship, and so we just lowered landing crafts and guys would get in -- in the crafts and pull out from the ship and drink, and then we'd swim, we'd dive on the landing craft and -- and swim that afternoon in the ocean there. And, uh, then that had -- that had one craft that would cruise back and forth with a couple of guys with M1 rifles watching for sharks {Laughing} while she swam. So -- and then another time we -- we pulled up to a -- a small deserted island. It was only maybe 100 yards wide, a couple hundred yards long. It was just a couple palm trees and sand, you know, and we had another -- put ashore and had another beer party and we built a fire and cooked hotdogs, and it was -- it was -- it was nice. So it was -- and you'd swim around -- around the shoal, coral and that, so -- but that was -- that's the only real fun thing that we -- that we did while we were over there. Then, of course, like I say, we went from, uh -- from Pearl Harbor then we went back to San Diego, and, of course, the war was still going on, so we were at San Diego getting re-outfitted and getting repairs, and while we were in San Diego the Japs surrendered, so there was no need for us to go back in the Pacific, so we got orders to go to Philadelphia. So we went down along the coast of California, Mexico, and then went through Panama Canal, which was -- was really neat, Panama, and up the coast, stopped at Panama -- Panama City and went ashore there for a couple of days, and then on up the coast and ended up in Philadelphia, the naval yard there, and our ship was then assigned to be decommissioned and scrapped. And I -- I was one of the first ones to take the first leave to go home, and so I left the ship and I never seen her again, because then, after my leave, I went to Maryland to pick up the new ship, the USS Fog, which -- which, of course, the war was already -- this was a new -- a new destroyer. It was -- it was designed for radar -- radar and -- and -- and what else -- we were experimenting with new types of radar, is what it was. And we did -- we did some -- worked with some care -- small carriers. I can remember one time we were escorting small carriers, they were teaching the -- the pilots how to land on the carrier, take off and landing, and then we would just stand by and pick up guys that crashed {laughing}. It was -- there wasn't a lot of them, but there was a couple of guys that would miss the ship for some reason or another and the carrier and crash, and we'd try to pick them up. But I seen -- we seen one -- one guy crashed and we never did get a chance to pick him up. We lost him. I -- I seen him -- I seen him floating by the ship, but then he -- then he just disappeared. And also we -- we did some duty with -- they were using radio controlled drones. They were about ten foot long wing span of 12, 15 feet, I don't know which, and they were radio controlled off the carrier, and the gunners would target practice on these drones, and then we would -- when they'd hit one down we'd go pick up the drone and recover it, and that was it. So most of the time on the Fog was -- we did -- I did service down in Key West, Florida, which was nice because it was in January -- January and February, and we went up -- up the -- on up the coast, stopped at -- what was it -- it's that big naval base on the east coast --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: New Port News?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah, but what's the city there? I forget. Any -- anyway, we stopped there for a while and then got over -- we went on up to New York. We spent a few days in New -- some time in New York and then from there went up to Portland, Maine, and then from there I got my orders to be discharged and I went -- went down to Boston, and they discharged me from Boston --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- and that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War II does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Mmm, oh, I don't know {laughing}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything that you haven't talked about that just kind of pops into your mind when you think about it?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Not offhand, it doesn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you -- How about mail call? Did you get many letters from home?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't get a lot because they couldn't --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, we were out of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- couldn't catch --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- out at sea most of the time. We didn't -- we weren't in -- in shore that long --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- so we didn't get much mail. And my parents weren't people that liked to write letters, so I didn't -- I didn't hardly get any mail.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they couldn't -- because you were a smaller ship, they didn't necessarily catch up with you, was that what it was?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, because we were -- just weren't available --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, just --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You had to go into port --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- to get mail?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: There was a standing -- standing joke amongst -- whenever a new guy came on board ship, you know, the old-timers would say "We want you to stand up in front and watch for the mail boy" --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- you know, and, of course, us dummies, you know, would "Oh, yeah, okay," you know, and you'd stand up there waiting for the mail boy so he could pick up the mail.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Finally -- you finally would realize, you know, there was no such thing as a mail boy, oh, but -- the only -- the only time we would get mail was -- all I can -- the time I can remember was when we went back to Hollandia. That was in New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: That was the big base there, and we picked up some mail then. And I don't -- I don't ever remember any -- I don't know if we received any from some supply ships or not that would catch up to us and give us mail. There weren't many times that we had any mail. So -- But as far as experiences, I -- nothing is very vivid anymore, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: I have to kind of think about -- about everything that happened, and -- and so it -- the only thing that was vivid was -- was the times when -- when our lives were actually in danger, you know. But I can see why they don't -- they don't draft old men. You know, when you're 18, 19 years old you're not afraid of anything, you know. I -- I -- you see all this stuff happening, the Japs coming down, the planes and everything, but I don't know, for some -- you must have something built inside of you that tells you, you know, you don't have to worry, you know, and so -- I don't -- I don't know if everybody felt that way, but I think you're too preoccupied with other things, I guess, to worry, you know, whether you're going to get killed or not. So other -- other than -- other than the times we were actually in danger, I don't -- there's nothing -- nothing stands out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies onboard ship, any particularly close buddies?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Well, I had -- I had those four guys from Warren.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You still hung around with those guys?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: No, you know, after the war we never contacted them again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. But you were pretty close on the ship?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Because we were from the same town, you know, sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know them before you in?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: A couple of them I did, yeah. But after the war, no, I lost touch with those -- Of course, what happened was I was from Warren, my wife here is from Cleveland. I was up visiting a cousin who was living upstairs from her mom and dad's house --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- and I met my wife. I was still in the service --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- so when I came home from the service I went home, but I didn't stay home very long. We were -- we got engaged while I was still in the service, and then when I came home I came up immediately to Cleveland and made arrangements to get married.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So I never went back to Warren. So I just made Cleveland my home. So -- So I never got back to -- Well, I guess everybody was that way, you know. I know her -- her brother, who was a combat engineer, he had guys right in -- right in Cleveland here, and they never got in touch with one another after the war. So I guess that happens to everybody. I don't know why. I guess everybody wants to forget --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- or something. I don't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What you just came back from?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Something like that. I don't know. Well -- So, you know, talking about -- talking about it over you questioning me, it doesn't sound -- {laughing} -- it doesn't sound very exciting, you know. You know, I just can't put the spin on it. I can't -- It's not as dramatic as you think it was going to be, you know. Unless you're actually there and -- and you see all these planes coming down and bursting in flames and hitting the ocean there next to you and your -- all your guns are going at one time, you know, it just -- other than that, you just try to talk about it, it's not like a -- like a movie, you know. You can't make it -- I can't make it sound real.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, it sounds very real {laughing}.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: So anyhow, well, it's -- it's my experiences, anyway. Yeah. Like I say, the only interesting -- really interesting part was -- was the -- about the story of the Ward --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- that's all -- that's the interesting -- that these started with the first shot in -- in at Pearl Harbor and ended up in Pearl -- 7th -- December 7th up there in Ormoc or Mindoro -- I forgot which one it was now -- and being sunk by its own -- own Captain -- a Captain that was on the Ward during Pearl Harbor --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He was on a different ship and --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- he was on the O'Brien, and he got the orders to sink the ship. That was interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you mentioned how -- how much action there was on that day. Was -- were the Japanese stepping up the action on that particular day because it was December 7th?

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: I don't know if that would have been -- could have been the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Whether they were trying to make a statement or --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Maybe. I don't know. But it didn't let up all day long, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: It was just one plane after another. There were a lot of ships that got hit that day, yeah. And a lot of them were -- well, a lot of them were knocked down by the air force, you know, Major Bong, those P38's, and -- and there was some Corsairs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Spell his name.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: Bong. B-o --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: B-o --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- n-g. Yeah. I got a picture of him downstairs --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- that I shot --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've heard about --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- in his P38.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lieutenant O'Hare --

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: But -- oh, yeah, he was a big ace over there. I forget -- forget how many planes he shot down, but after the war he came back to the states and was a test pilot in California for one of the air -- big aircraft companies, and he got killed --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: John Szakacs
sp.p: -- testing just a short time after he came home. Isn't that ironic?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.
